newsitem.title: POLAND: Untested Polish finance chief vows further reform.
newsitem.headline: Untested Polish finance chief vows further reform.

text.p: Poland's new Finance Minister Marek Belka on Tuesday vowed to maintain the country's high economic growth rate, curb inflation and control the budget deficit.
Belka, 45, was appointed earlier in the day to replace Grzegorz Kolodko, who quit saying he did not want to be drawn into campaigning for parliamentary elections due in the autumn.

"My policy will be that of full and active continuation of a policy of macroeconomic consolidation, fighting inflation and controlling the budget," Belka, an independent economist, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"I would like to participate more actively in the speeding up of several structural reforms awaiting us," he said, adding he would pay special attention to bank privatisation and the long-delayed overhaul of the creaking social security system.

Belka had been economic adviser to President Aleksander Kwasniewski since 1995, when Kwasniewski beat incumbent Lech Walesa in the presidential polls, but has no previous experience in a top government post.

Belka said he would not seek to cut inflation at all costs because such a policy would bring economic collapse, but added that price growth must be curbed if Poland's economic growth was to be maintained.
"Fast economic growth cannot be sustained with inflation at current levels -- it has to be reduced for growth to be permanent," Belka said.
Year-on-year inflation fell to 18.5 percent last year from 21.6 percent in 1995 and the budget draft for this year sees it falling to 13 percent in December 1997.
Gross domestic product (GDP) rose six percent last year after seven percent growth in 1995 and the government has forecast 5.5 percent growth this year.

Belka said that although he did not participate in drafting the 1997 budget law, he fully supported its goals. "Everything has to be done to reach the (inflation, GDP growth) goals envisaged by the budget," he said.
Leszek Balcerowicz, head of the opposition Union for Freedom party and architect of the market reforms started in 1989, praised Belka's knowledge but said was he was untested in the policy hot seat.

"I know Professor Marek Belka as very a good economist who knows western economy well, but I cannot say anything about his ability to make decisions in difficult matters such as economic policy," Balcerowicz told the private Radio Zet.
Western diplomats said that although they were sorry to see Kolodko go, Belka's appointment was not a cause for concern.

"Mr Belka has very sound views, convictions and with such background he is extremely suited (for the post), although he can be tested only on the job," said a senior representative of an international financial institution.
"He is a straight continuation of what has made Poland do well over the past seven years, which is a basic consensus on sound finance and market-oriented structural reforms," he said.

Belka is an economics professor at the Polish Academy of Sciences specialising in banking and monetary policies. He has written books on Milton Friedman and the economic policies of the Reagan administration.

"I highly value Mr Belka as an economist. He has an open and inquiring mind, is precise in presenting his views and is a pleasure to work with," Bogdan Wyznikiewicz, head of the Gdansk Institute for Market Economy think tank, told Radio Zet.

Belka was a World Bank and International Finance Corporation (IFC) consultant from 1991 to 1993 and a finance ministry consultant from 1992 to 1993. For six months he lectured at the London School of Economics. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
